title: sorting
quote: Electre Tri is a set of methods designed to sort alternatives evaluated on several criteria into ordered categories.
context: Multi-criteria SORTING: a decision maker defines ordered categories by reference profiles; each alternative is assigned by comparison with them. Profiles and thresholds are elicited from the decision maker.
transfer: Direct fit: results are sorted into ordered categories — fits (base) > option (trade-off) > rejected. A category may have several limiting profiles: the BASE profile (every asked requirement incl. the anchor, e.g. the asked brands) and an OPTION profile (anchor partly missing, every other purpose requirement at a high level). Condition: profiles come from the asker's words, hints and the purpose, are shown to the owner and editable — never invented by the engine alone.

title: alternatives
quote: OR-refinement links relate a goal to an alternative set of refinements; this means that satisfying one of the refinements is sufficient for satisfying the parent goal.
context: Requirements engineering for SYSTEM design: alternative refinements are alternative designs to satisfy a system goal; chosen by analysts.
transfer: Transfer by analogy only: a purpose goal of the asker ("guests come for the natural setting") may be met by alternative means (sea near OR scenic surroundings). Condition: the parent goal is found by WHY from the asker's words/purpose; alternatives are proposed, voted and owner-confirmed; the asker's own requirement always stays one alternative. Does not license dropping an asker's must-have.

title: LLM reliability
quote: In addition, when evaluated by human annotators, GPT-4o generates goal model refinement relationships among extracted goals with 72.2% accuracy.
context: Goals extracted from stakeholder interview transcripts, judged by human annotators.
transfer: A model-proposed refinement (alternative, category profile) is wrong about 1 time in 4 in that setting: every such proposal needs independent-family votes (#212) and owner confirmation before it can change which items count.

title: means vs ends
quote: not verified on the original text
context: Structuring a decision maker's own objectives: means objectives matter only through fundamental objectives, found by asking "why is this important?".
transfer: Supporting only; never the sole basis of a rule until a quote is verified on an open text.

title: trade-offs
quote: not verified on the original text
context: The decision maker makes each trade-off; dominated alternatives are eliminated.
transfer: Supporting only: OPTIONS are shown with what they give up (the missing anchor) and what they gain, so the OWNER makes the trade-off; the engine never counts an option as meeting every must-have.

title: verifier
quote: We argue that auto-regressive LLMs cannot, by themselves, do planning or self-verification (which is after all a form of reasoning), and shed some light on the reasons for misunderstandings in the literature.
transfer: Every model output is a proposal; it counts after a code check

title: domain knowledge
quote: Zave and Jackson’s famous conceptualization of requirements engineering, that is, K, S ⊢ R
transfer: Domain knowledge is a slot of the request model, not background

title: goal → metric
quote: GQM goals are defined in terms of purpose, focus, object of study, viewpoint, and context.
transfer: Each requirement carries viewpoint and context (roles) and a measure

title: LLM goal extraction
quote: Although the pipeline achieved 61% accuracy in low-level goal identification, the final stage, these results indicate the approach is best suited as a tool to accelerate manual extraction rather than as a full replacement.
transfer: The request model is checked by a second family and by trace gates

title: implicit requirements
quote: Evaluating 16 frontier and open-weight models across 205 scenarios, we find that even the best-performing model achieves only 48.3% scenario pass rate, revealing substantial room for improvement in bridging the gap between literal instruction-following and human-like contextual reasoning.
transfer: Implicit requirements stated and labelled derived

title: checklists
quote: We demonstrate that using TICK leads to a significant increase (46.4% $\to$ 52.2%) in the frequency of exact agreements between LLM judgements and human preferences, as compared to having an LLM directly score an output.
transfer: Hard checks in small batches

title: early stopping
quote: Averaged over five reasoning benchmarks, CGES reduces the average number of calls by 58% on average (from 16.0 to 6.7) while matching its accuracy within 0.4 percentage points of self-consistency.
transfer: Second opinions stop at agreement

title: plan once
quote: Evaluation across multiple real-world agent applications shows that our system can reduce costs by 50.31% and latency by 27.28% on average while maintaining performance, offering a more efficient solution for serving LLM-based agents that complements existing LLM serving infrastructures.
transfer: Decompose once, every stage reads it; reuse per kind

title: early pruning
quote: Our results show that pruning effectiveness depends more on where pruning is applied than on the specific scoring rule: early pruning yields the largest end-to-end savings, while later pruning mainly refines the final synthesis context.
transfer: Code checks before page judging

title: self-improvement
quote: Across six tasks, GEPA outperforms GRPO by 6% on average and by up to 20%, while using up to 35x fewer rollouts.
transfer: Loop proposals reflect on failing traces; lessons as itemised playbook

title: eval statistics
quote: Evaluations are critical for understanding the capabilities of large language models (LLMs).
transfer: Reference gate compares paired with intervals

title: tidy data
quote: Each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each type of observational unit is a table.
context: Wickham, Tidy Data, J. Stat. Software 59(10), 2014 — tidy datasets are easy to manipulate, model and visualize because they have a specific structure.
transfer: Observation tables follow tidy data principles: each row is one observation (time × entity), each column a variable with its unit, and the table represents one observational unit. The spec proposes columns from the asker's words and code enforces them.

title: LLM forecasting ablation
quote: removing the LLM component or replacing it with a basic attention layer does not degrade forecasting performance
context: Tan et al., Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?, NeurIPS 2024 — ablation studies on three LLM-based forecasting methods show the LLM adds no value; the forecast is computed by code, never by a model.
transfer: The forecast operation is pure code (drift + seasonal naive + Theil–Sen trend), no model call. The model only proposes the table spec and extracts observations with quotes; all aggregation, trend, and forecast are deterministic code.

title: simple forecasting benchmarks
quote: A variation on the naïve method is to allow the forecasts to increase or decrease over time, where the amount of change over time (called the drift) is set to be the average change seen in the historical data.
context: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice — seasonal naïve and drift as benchmark methods. Seasonal naïve: each forecast equals the last observed value from the same season. Drift: extrapolates the line between first and last observations.
transfer: Forecast uses drift with Theil–Sen slope as the trend, plus seasonal naïve offsets when ≥12 periods exist. Interval from residual quantiles (10–90%) of the fitted series. Never a model call.

title: retrieval-augmented forecasting
quote: We build a retrieval-augmented LM system that significantly improves upon the baseline and approaches the human crowd performance on competitive forecasting platforms.
context: Halawi et al., Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models, 2024 — retrieval-augmented LM system searches for relevant information, generates forecasts, and aggregates predictions. The system uses retrieval-augmented reasoning for explanations (drivers), not for the numbers.
transfer: Drivers (reasons with justification) come from the pieces as labelled explanations; the model proposes them but they are traced to source quotes. The numbers (observations, aggregates, trend, forecast) are computed by code. Memocheck treats forecast numbers as code-computed.
